title: Banks as Custodians, Not Arbiters: Karnataka High Court Reaffirms Proportionality in Account Freezing Orders
description:
In a landmark judgment (Sri. Madhu v. IndusInd Bank Ltd. & Anr., 9th June 2026), the Karnataka High Court definitively ruled that banking institutions, when acting on freezing directions from investigating agencies, must strictly adhere to the specified scope and quantum of those directions. The Court clarified that a bank cannot unilaterally extend a freeze to an entire account based merely on the apprehension of receiving further directives in the future, thus circumscribing the limits of a bank's authority in such scenarios.

The case arose from IndusInd Bank freezing the petitioner Sri. Madhu's entire account, despite receiving specific requests from two different police stations totaling Rs. 25,000/-. The bank justified its full account freeze by citing the possibility of additional freezing requests from other agencies. Aggrieved by this disproportionate action, Sri. Madhu petitioned the High Court, challenging the bank's arbitrary exercise of power and seeking to unfreeze amounts exceeding the directed sum.

Justice Suraj Govindaraj's ruling underscored that a bank's power in implementing a freeze is derivative and ministerial, not independent. A bank functions as a custodian, obligated to implement only what is lawfully directed, and its authority is co-extensive with the terms of the received directions. The Court emphatically rejected the bank's apprehension of future directives as a valid legal basis, stating that administrative convenience and anticipatory action cannot substitute a subsisting legal mandate. Crucially, the judgment invoked the principle of proportionality, asserting that any restriction on a bank account must precisely correspond to the extent of the direction received.

Consequently, the High Court allowed the petition, directing the debit freeze to be restricted solely to the aggregate amount of Rs. 25,000/-, permitting the petitioner to operate the remaining balance and future credits. The Court further issued a prospective direction to IndusInd Bank, stipulating that in all future cases, it must strictly adhere to the tenor of directions received, earmarking only the specified sum unless a complete freeze is explicitly mandated or statutorily required. This judgment powerfully reaffirms that banks occupy a strictly ministerial role, upholding legal rights over administrative convenience.

title: Jayakrishna Menon v. Krishnankutty & Ors.
description:
The Supreme Court, in Jayakrishna Menon v. Krishnankutty & Ors. (June 9, 2026), issued a stern ruling on contempt of court and animal welfare. The case stemmed from a custody dispute over Raman, Kerala's tallest captive elephant, and focused on the alleged wilful disobedience of a solemn undertaking given to the Court.

The petitioner, Jayakrishna Menon, claimed Raman belonged to the Mata Amritanandamayi Mutt and had been entrusted to Respondent No. 1, Krishnankutty, solely for care. Krishnankutty, however, asserted ownership, leading to criminal proceedings and a protracted legal battle. During pending appeals before the Supreme Court, Krishnankutty's counsel explicitly undertook on August 6, 2025, that Raman would not be used for any commercial or temple activities in the interim.

Despite this undertaking, the petitioner alleged Raman's continued deployment in temple festivals and public events. Respondent No. 1 initially denied the allegations but later admitted in written submissions that Raman participated in a "brief ceremonial ritual" at a temple, attributing it to veterinary advice for walks and another elephant's illness. A State inspection report subsequently corroborated Raman's presence at a temple festival, confirming the breach.

The Court found the violation of the undertaking "beyond dispute," established by Respondent No. 1's admission and the State's report. Expressing profound concern over the commercial exploitation of Raman in defiance of its order, the Court emphasized its duty towards voiceless beings, stating it could not be a "mute spectator" to such conduct. State authorities, however, were discharged, as their attempts to inspect were deemed genuine despite initial challenges.

Consequently, the Supreme Court held Respondent No. 1 guilty of contempt of court for wilful disobedience and imposed a fine of INR 2,000. Crucially, prioritizing Raman's health and welfare pending final adjudication, the Court directed the State of Kerala to take temporary custody of the elephant, house him in an appropriate rescue or rehabilitation centre, and care for him at its expense. This judgment powerfully reaffirms the sanctity of judicial undertakings and highlights the judiciary's proactive role in safeguarding animal welfare.

title: NCLAT Upholds CIRP Against Rana Kapoor-Linked Companies: Debt, Default and the Limits of Arbitration Challenges under the IBC
description:
The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) reinforced the creditor-friendly framework of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) in `Bindu Kapoor v. Sapan Mohan Garg (IRP) & Ors.`. It dismissed appeals by Bindu Kapoor, upholding the admission of Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) against Bliss Abode Pvt. Ltd. and Bliss House Pvt. Ltd., companies linked to Rana Kapoor.

The dispute stemmed from loan facilities by Indiabulls Housing Finance to the companies, personally guaranteed by Rana and Bindu Kapoor. Rana Kapoor's arrest in March 2020 triggered "material adverse effect" clauses in the agreements, leading to loan recall notices. Failure to repay resulted in arbitration proceedings, culminating in awards favouring the lender in February 2023. Subsequently, the debt was assigned to JC Flowers Asset Reconstruction, which initiated Section 7 IBC proceedings, which the NCLT admitted and NCLAT upheld.

The NCLAT rejected the appellant's challenges. It affirmed the loan recall's validity, finding the "material adverse effect" clause properly invoked due to Rana Kapoor's situation genuinely impacting repayment capacity. The Tribunal clarified that pending challenges to arbitral awards before the Delhi High Court did not preclude insolvency proceedings; the primary default was non-compliance with the 2020 recall notices, with arbitral awards serving only as additional evidence of debt and default.

Additionally, NCLAT distinguished IBC proceedings from mere execution actions, noting it wasn't a disguised recovery attempt given the prolonged non-repayment. It reiterated the limited scope of Section 7—to ascertain the existence of financial debt and default, not equitable considerations—relying on Supreme Court precedents. The NCLAT also confirmed that an arbitral award creates a fresh cause of action, rendering the Section 7 applications timely. This judgment significantly reinforces contractual default provisions and the IBC's effectiveness as a resolution mechanism, irrespective of parallel recovery disputes.

title: The Sole Surviving Widow’s Right to Full Family Pension: A Clarification by the Punjab and Haryana High Court
description:
In a pivotal judgment delivered on May 22, 2026, the Punjab and Haryana High Court, in *Manjit Kaur v. State of Punjab & Others*, conclusively held that a sole surviving widow of a deceased government employee is entitled to 100% family pension, irrespective of her status as the second wife. This ruling resolves a longstanding interpretive controversy surrounding Notes 1 and 2 appended to Rule 6.17(4) of the Punjab Civil Services Rules, Volume II, and reaffirms that the State cannot misappropriate any portion of the family pension due to the legal heirs.

The petitioner, Smt. Manjit Kaur, was the second wife of Sh. Parshotam Lal Puri, a retired District Treasury Officer. His first wife had predeceased him in 1980, and a Legal Heir Certificate confirmed Smt. Manjit Kaur as the sole eligible claimant with no eligible minor children from the first marriage. Despite this, the Accountant General restricted her family pension to 50%, citing her status as the ‘second wife’ and invoking Notes 1 and 2 of the relevant rules.

Justice Namit Kumar meticulously examined these rules, finding them inapplicable. Note 1 applies only when an employee is survived by *more than one widow simultaneously*, a condition absent here as the first wife died decades earlier. Note 2's operation is premised on the existence of an *eligible minor child from a pre-deceased wife*, which was also not the case. The Court emphasized that apportionment rules are designed to distribute pension among multiple *simultaneous claimants*, not to reduce the share of a sole eligible heir. Relying on precedents like *Harpal Kaur* and *Ram Dulari*, the Court affirmed that the State cannot retain any portion of the family pension.

Consequently, the High Court allowed the writ petition, setting aside the impugned memo and declaring Smt. Manjit Kaur entitled to 100% family pension from November 14, 2011, along with arrears and 6% interest. This significant judgment clarifies that pension apportionment rules cannot be misapplied to penalize a sole surviving widow, even if a second wife, when the conditions for multiple claimants are not met, ensuring the full benefit reaches the deceased employee's family.

title: Unilateral Appointment of Arbitrators Under Section 12(5) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996: A Critical Analysis of Air Force Naval Housing Board v. M/s N G Constructions
description:
The Delhi High Court, in Air Force Naval Housing Board v. M/s N G Constructions (2026), delivered a landmark ruling on the unilateral appointment of arbitrators under Section 12(5) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The case arose from a construction contract where the Air Force Naval Housing Board unilaterally appointed a sole arbitrator, as per a contractual clause. Subsequently, the Board itself sought to set aside the arbitral award, arguing that its own appointment violated Section 12(5) read with the Seventh Schedule of the Act, which mandates automatic ineligibility for party-employees or their nominees.

Justice Avneesh Jhingan, citing Supreme Court decisions like Bhadra International and the Delhi High Court's Mahavir Prasad Gupta, affirmed that Section 12(5) renders such unilateral appointments void ab initio. These precedents establish that the ineligibility stems from operation of law, ensuring equal treatment of parties. Crucially, the Court reiterated that the proviso to Section 12(5) demands an "express agreement in writing" for waiver, which cannot be inferred from a party's participation in proceedings or conduct. Such conduct is inconsequential and cannot cure the statutory defect. Furthermore, the judgment upheld that even the party making the unilateral appointment retains the right to challenge the award, as the tribunal's inherent lack of jurisdiction renders the proceedings a nullity.

Consequently, the Court allowed the petition, setting aside the impugned award dated 27th July 2022. This ruling robustly reinforces the legislative intent of the 2015 Amendment, ensuring impartiality and integrity in the arbitral process. It clarifies that fundamental jurisdictional defects arising from statutory ineligibility cannot be overcome by implied consent or acquiescence, serving as a critical precedent, especially for unilateral appointment clauses prevalent in government contracts.

title: Mandatory Compliance with Rule 9 of SARFAESI Rules: Supreme Court Quashes Sixteen-Year-Old Auction Sale for Statutory Non-Compliance
description:
In a landmark judgment, the Supreme Court of India in M.R. Vasumathi v. Authorized Officer and Ors. reaffirmed the mandatory nature of procedural safeguards under the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002 (SARFAESI Act). The Court quashed a sixteen-year-old auction sale of a mortgaged property due to non-compliance with Rule 9 of the Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, 2002, despite concurrent findings by lower tribunals and the Madras High Court.

The case originated from a 1984 loan default, leading to a preliminary decree in 1997. Following the guarantor's death, Indian Bank invoked SARFAESI in 2009. The auction in 2010 saw the successful bidder pay 25% immediately, but the remaining 75% was paid beyond the stipulated 15-day period, and crucially, without a written agreement for extension as mandated by Rule 9(4). The legal heirs challenged this, but their petitions were dismissed by the DRT, DRAT, and High Court, citing delay and borrower indolence.

The Supreme Court emphasized that auction validity hinges strictly on statutory compliance, not equitable considerations. It ruled that Rule 9(3) (immediate 25% deposit) and Rule 9(4) (balance within 15 days or written extension) are mandatory, not merely directory. The Court found the balance payment on March 31, 2010, was ex facie beyond the March 26, 2010 deadline and lacked any written agreement for extension, rendering the sale invalid. It held that statutory non-compliance cannot be waived or regularized by the secured creditor.

Invoking its equitable jurisdiction under Article 142, the Supreme Court quashed the auction sale. It directed a full refund of the deposited amount to the auction purchaser with 7% interest. Concurrently, it granted the appellant, the legal heir, a one-time opportunity to redeem the mortgage by paying the original outstanding amount plus 5% interest. This judgment underscores strict adherence to SARFAESI procedural mandates, while balancing equities through Article 142 to ensure justice and protect parties' interests.

title: Vandana Garg (RP) v. Mysore Petro Chemicals: Scope of Section 14 Moratorium and the Survival of Underlying Real Estate Claims in CIRP
description:
The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) in *Vandana Garg (RP) v. Mysore Petro Chemicals* clarified the absolute nature of the Section 14 moratorium under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), particularly regarding the creation of new liabilities. The case involved Mysore Petro Chemicals, an allottee, who sought to admit a claim in the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of Raghuleela Builders (Corporate Debtor).

Mysore Petro Chemicals had invested ₹12.93 crore for a commercial unit in 2015. When the Corporate Debtor failed to deliver, Mysore Petro Chemicals appealed to the Maharashtra Real Estate Regulatory Appellate Authority (RERAA) in December 2020. Critically, the Corporate Debtor was admitted into CIRP on October 4, 2021, triggering the moratorium. Despite this, RERAA passed an ex-parte order in June 2022, directing the Corporate Debtor to pay compensation. The Resolution Professional (RP) rejected the claim based on this post-moratorium RERAA order, citing Section 14 and belated submission. The NCLT, however, admitted the claim.

The NCLAT, overturning the NCLT's decision, held that the RERAA order, having been passed during the subsistence of the moratorium (October 2021 - June 2022) and creating a *new compensation liability*, was ineffective against the Corporate Debtor. Relying on *P. Mohanraj*, the Tribunal emphasized that Section 14(1)(a) prohibits the continuation of proceedings that create fresh liabilities against the Corporate Debtor, distinguishing it from *ABG Shipyard* which allows adjudication of pre-existing liabilities in certain contexts. The issue of belated claim submission was deemed academic since the foundational RERAA order itself was void against the Corporate Debtor.

However, the NCLAT adopted an equitable approach, acknowledging that the IBC is not expropriatory. While the claim based on the RERAA order was not maintainable, the Tribunal recognized Mysore Petro Chemicals' underlying bona fide investment. It directed the RP to verify the ₹12.93 crore payment from the Corporate Debtor's records and include it as a claim. This judgment underscores the stringent scope of the Section 14 moratorium against new liabilities while reinforcing the RP's duty to identify and recognize genuine underlying claims, even in the absence of strict formal compliance with claim timelines.

title: The Limitation Clock Starts with Inquiry, Not Ignorance: Supreme Court on Probate Revocation
description:
The Supreme Court, in Dhiraj Dutta v. Anirban Sen & Ors., ruled that the limitation period for probate revocation begins with constructive notice, not merely actual knowledge. This significant decision clarified the interplay between Section 263 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, and Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, reaffirming that the law aids the vigilant.

The case involved an application filed in 2022 to revoke a probate granted in 1995, nearly three decades earlier. The respondents, who were nephews-in-law of the testatrix, claimed they only discovered the probate's existence in 2019. However, the appellant had initiated mutation proceedings in 2010-11, and notices concerning these proceedings were served to the respondents' predecessors-in-interest in 2013.

The Court determined that while Section 263 allows revocation for "just cause," it lacks a specific limitation period, thus invoking Article 137 of the Limitation Act, which prescribes a three-year period from when the "right to apply accrues." Crucially, the Supreme Court held that the notices served during the 2013 mutation proceedings constituted constructive notice of the appellant's probated claim. A "reasonably prudent person" receiving such notices affecting their property rights would have diligently inquired into the basis of these proceedings, which would have revealed the probate.

By choosing to ignore these notices, the respondents failed to exercise due diligence. Consequently, the Court concluded that the limitation period commenced in 2013, making their 2022 revocation application hopelessly time-barred. This judgment reinforces that parties cannot indefinitely postpone legal challenges by claiming ignorance when circumstances reasonably require inquiry, thereby strengthening the finality and certainty attached to probate grants.

title: The Inherent Boundaries of Justice: Section 528 BNSS and the Limits of Pre-Trial Quashing in Cheque Dishonour Cases
description:
The Punjab and Haryana High Court, in Atul Vig v. Hunny Singh Ahluwalia & Anr., provided a crucial exposition on the interplay between the High Court's inherent jurisdiction under Section 528 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), and the statutory framework for cheque dishonour cases under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The judgment firmly reiterates that pre-trial quashing of a criminal complaint is an exceptional remedy, not a substitute for a full trial.

The case involved a complainant alleging that the petitioner dishonoured two cheques totaling Rs. 49 lakhs, issued against a friendly loan. The petitioner sought quashing, arguing the loan's undocumented cash nature, its fiscal impermissibility, and inconsistencies in the loan agreement. Crucially, the petitioner contended the cheques were forcibly extracted through coercion linked to a failed property transaction, supported by a prior police complaint alleging duress.

The High Court, drawing upon the principles governing inherent jurisdiction, emphasized its sparing and cautious exercise. It noted that the petitioner did not deny signing or issuing the cheques. This non-denial automatically triggered the statutory presumptions under Sections 118 and 139 of the NI Act, which posit that the cheque was issued in discharge of a legally enforceable debt. Rebutting these presumptions, including the coercion plea, constitutes disputed questions of fact that require the adduction of evidence during a trial. The court also observed that the police complaint alleging coercion lacked material demonstrating any further pursuit or action taken upon it.

Finding no merit in the petition, the High Court dismissed it. This decision underscores that the remedy of quashing is not intended to insulate an accused from trial where disputed questions of fact are involved. The non-denial of signatures on a dishonoured cheque, coupled with the operation of statutory presumptions, creates a strong prima facie case that necessitates adjudication through the trial process, thereby preserving the integrity of the Section 138 mechanism as a commercial remedy.

title: Scope and Limits of Section 11 Adjudication: The Delhi High Court on Prima Facie Arbitration Agreements, Waiver, and Parallel Proceedings
description:
The Delhi High Court, in *VE Commercial Vehicles Limited v. Singh Enterprises* (30th May 2026), delivered a significant ruling clarifying the scope of Section 11 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The judgment addressed complex questions concerning arbitration jurisdiction, seat determination, and the interplay between civil litigation and IBC proceedings arising from a terminated commercial dealership agreement.

The dispute commenced when VE Commercial Vehicles (petitioner) invoked arbitration after terminating a dealership agreement with Singh Enterprises (respondent) due to alleged non-compliance and outstanding payments. Singh Enterprises vigorously opposed the arbitration petition, contending the agreement was unexecuted, alleging forgery of signatures to alter contract terms (leading to a criminal complaint), and claiming the petitioner had waived its arbitration rights by previously filing two civil suits. Respondents also challenged the Delhi High Court's territorial jurisdiction, asserting exclusive jurisdiction of Indore courts, and highlighted a subsequent Section 8 IBC notice.

The Court meticulously analyzed Clause 34 of the Dealership Agreement, which stipulated Delhi as the "place of arbitration" and made Indore's exclusive jurisdiction "subject to" this arbitration clause. Relying on Supreme Court precedents, the Court unequivocally held that Delhi was the juridical seat, emphasizing party autonomy in seat selection. Regarding the validity of the arbitration agreement and forgery allegations, the Court ruled that at the Section 11 stage, its jurisdiction was limited to examining the *prima facie* existence of an arbitration agreement, not adjudicating disputed facts like fraud or forgery. It noted that the respondents themselves had invoked the arbitration clause, and the alleged forgery concerned only the term duration, not the arbitration agreement itself.

The Court rejected the waiver argument, finding that a withdrawn civil suit (with liberty to institute fresh proceedings) and another suit concerning a distinct cause of action did not constitute an irrevocable waiver of arbitration rights. Similarly, the IBC notice, issued *after* the arbitration invocation and not followed by formal insolvency proceedings, was deemed a "counter-blast" against the petitioner's legitimate claims. Consequently, the Court exercised its power under Section 11 to appoint Justice (Retd.) Kurian Joseph as the Presiding Arbitrator, preserving all substantive contentions for determination by the arbitral tribunal.

This judgment robustly affirms arbitration as a preferred dispute resolution mechanism, upholding party autonomy in seat selection, and maintaining the limited scope of judicial intervention at the Section 11 stage. It provides crucial clarity on resolving seat-venue conflicts, the treatment of IBC notices issued after arbitration invocation, and the impact of withdrawn or distinct civil suits on arbitration rights.

title: The 60-Day Wall: Supreme Court Affirms Inflexible Limitation Regime Under Section 62 of the IBC
description:
The Supreme Court of India, in CA Ramchandra Dallaram Choudhary (Liquidator) v. Adani Infrastructure & Developers Pvt. Ltd., has definitively reinforced the absolute and non-negotiable nature of the limitation regime under Section 62 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016. This landmark judgment underscores the Code's fundamental principles of expedition, finality, and discipline in corporate insolvency resolution, establishing that IBC timelines are stringent statutory requirements, not flexible guidelines.

The Court clarified that Section 62 mandates appeals to be filed within 45 days, with a strictly limited grace period of 15 additional days only for "sufficient cause," thereby imposing an absolute outer limit of 60 days. Beyond this period, the Court's jurisdiction to condone delay is entirely ousted. Furthermore, while the Supreme Court Rules (SCR) permit 28 days for curing defects in an appeal, this period is also a strict deadline. The Court explicitly ruled that filing a defective appeal to circumvent limitation, followed by a leisurely approach to curing defects, is impermissible and undermines the statutory scheme of the IBC.

Arguments seeking leniency, such as the Liquidator's status as a neutral officer or the invocation of Article 142 of the Constitution, were firmly rejected. The Court emphasized that the IBC is a complete code regarding appeals, and the SCR, as subordinate legislation, cannot override its express provisions. A previous indulgence granted by a coordinate bench in a Section 61 appeal was specifically noted as non-precedential, reinforcing that serial condonations across successive appellate stages are not countenanced by the law of limitation under the IBC.

Ultimately, the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal as time-barred. It asserted that once the 60-day window under the IBC, coupled with the 28-day defect-curing period under the SCR, expires, the right to appeal is irrevocably extinguished. This judgment serves as a clear directive, cementing the 60-day ceiling and the 28-day defect-curing period as an impermeable barrier crucial for safeguarding the time-bound integrity and efficacy of the IBC process.

title: Passport Denial Based on FIR Alone Impermissible, Rules Andhra Pradesh High Court
description:
The Andhra Pradesh High Court has ruled that denying a passport based solely on a First Information Report (FIR) or an ongoing police investigation is impermissible. Interpreting Section 6(2)(f) of the Passports Act, 1967, the Court clarified that the statutory embargo applies only when "proceedings in respect of an offence... are pending before a criminal court in India," which necessitates the court having taken cognizance of the alleged offence.

The Court emphasized that mere registration of an FIR or pendency of an investigation does not constitute 'proceedings pending before a criminal court.' This decision reinforces fundamental rights, including the presumption of innocence and the constitutional right to travel abroad under Article 21. It prevents arbitrary administrative action, ensuring that personal liberty is not curtailed based on unproven allegations. The High Court directed passport authorities to process applications without treating a pending crime number as a disqualification until formal judicial proceedings commence with court cognizance, thus providing crucial clarity and safeguard against administrative overreach.

title: Can Borrowers Avoid Pre-Deposit in SARFAESI Appeals? Calcutta High Court Settles the Debate
description:
The Calcutta High Court, in Jainco Projects (India) Ltd. v. UCO Bank and Ors., unequivocally reaffirmed the mandatory nature of the pre-deposit requirement under Section 18 of the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002 (SARFAESI Act) for appeals. The Court clarified that borrowers cannot circumvent this statutory obligation, even if the appeal arises from an interlocutory order concerning a One Time Settlement (OTS) proposal.

The petitioner, Jainco Projects, had their application to compel UCO Bank to implement an OTS scheme rejected by the Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT). Challenging this, they appealed to the Debts Recovery Appellate Tribunal (DRAT) and sought a complete waiver of the Section 18 pre-deposit, arguing the DRT's order was merely procedural. The DRAT, however, directed a 50% deposit, which Jainco then contested before the Calcutta High Court under Article 227.

The High Court meticulously distinguished the case from Sunshine Builders, explaining that an order rejecting an OTS proposal directly impacts the borrower’s financial liability and the secured creditor’s recoverable dues, making it a substantive determination, not merely procedural. Orders affecting substantive rights, even if interlocutory, attract the mandatory pre-deposit under Section 18. The Court reiterated that this statutory provision creates an absolute bar against entertaining an appeal unless the prescribed deposit (50%, reducible to 25% by DRAT) is made, and neither the DRAT nor the High Court possesses the authority to waive it entirely.

Dismissing the petition, the High Court upheld the DRAT’s order. This judgment is crucial for clarifying the distinction between procedural and substantive orders for Section 18 purposes. It strengthens the principle that appellate remedies under the SARFAESI Act are conditional, not absolute, thereby discouraging frivolous litigation and ensuring the expeditious resolution of debt recovery proceedings. The ruling provides significant guidance for disputes involving OTS schemes and reinforces judicial adherence to the legislative objective of maintaining financial discipline and a structured appellate process.

title: DNA Testing and Paternity Disputes: The Supreme Court Reaffirms the Balance of Interests
description:
In Chaturbhuj Pradhan v. Amar Pradhan & Anr. (2026), the Supreme Court of India upheld a lower court's direction for DNA testing to determine paternity. This ruling re-emphasizes the legal framework for court-ordered DNA tests in civil proceedings, founded on evidentiary insufficiency and the balance of competing interests.

The case centered on Amar Pradhan, born in 1999, seeking paternity declaration against Chaturbhuj Pradhan (CP), who consistently denied fatherhood. After years of litigation, Amar, upon majority, filed a civil suit. Both trial and High Courts directed a DNA test, prompting CP's appeal based on objections like compelled testing, absence of "eminent need," and res judicata from prior summary maintenance proceedings.

Reviewing precedents, the Court affirmed DNA tests are exceptional, not routine, warranted only when paternity is unequivocally in issue and no other evidence provides a conclusive resolution. It reinforced the "balance of interests" framework, weighing the alleged father's privacy against the child's fundamental right to lineage and identity.

Dismissing CP's appeal, the Court found his prolonged paternity denial left no alternative proof, making the DNA test indispensable. It rejected the res judicata argument, clarifying that findings from summary criminal maintenance proceedings lack finality for a civil paternity suit. The Court held Amar's compelling right to establish parentage decisively outweighed CP's privacy interest, directing the trial court to proceed with the DNA examination.

This judgment underscores that judicial power to order DNA tests is circumscribed, exercised only when evidentiary alternatives are exhausted and the balance of interests demands it. It reinforces that privacy is not absolute, yielding to significant competing rights, and clarifies the limited precedential value of summary legal findings.

title: Karnataka High Court Directs Enforcement of K-RERA Recovery Certificates Within Eight Weeks
description:
The Karnataka High Court, in *Rajesh Rao C.V. and Others v. State of Karnataka and Others*, has decisively reiterated that recovery certificates issued by the Karnataka Real Estate Regulatory Authority (K-RERA) must be enforced promptly. The judgment, delivered on 27 April 2026, addresses a critical practical challenge where successful claimants under the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 (RERA Act), face delays in actual recovery despite obtaining valid certificates.

The petitioners approached the High Court seeking a writ of mandamus, contending that designated authorities had failed to act upon K-RERA recovery certificates issued against Respondent No. 6. They emphasized that Section 40 of the RERA Act and Rule 25 of the Karnataka Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Rules, 2017, mandate the recovery of such amounts as arrears of land revenue. The core grievance was that the issuance of certificates had not led to actual enforcement.

The Court consistently observed that once a recovery certificate is issued under RERA, the concerned authorities are under an undeniable obligation to recover the specified amount. It clarified that enforcement is not optional or discretionary, especially given the appointment of a Special Deputy Commissioner to handle such cases. The Court concluded that the petitioners had a clear legal right to demand enforcement, and the authorities had a corresponding duty.

Consequently, the High Court allowed the writ petition, issuing a writ of mandamus. It directed the respondent authorities to execute the recovery certificates and recover the amounts within eight weeks from the order's receipt. Furthermore, it granted petitioners the liberty to provide details of the debtor's properties to assist the Special Deputy Commissioner in the recovery process.

This judgment holds significant importance as it reinforces the enforceability of RERA-issued recovery certificates, ensuring that administrative inaction does not undermine regulatory relief. It strengthens the RERA Act's implementation mechanism by making authorities accountable and translating adjudicatory orders into actual recovery for beneficiaries, affirming that a recovery certificate is an enforceable statutory instrument.

title: Misrepresentation of Age in Matrimonial Alliances: Legal Remedies and Procedural Rigor in Family Court Appeals
description:
The Telangana High Court, in F.C.A. No. 226 of 2024, addressed a matrimonial dispute centered on fraudulent age misrepresentation and the procedural rigor for ancillary reliefs. The appellant wife sought annulment of her 2018 marriage, alleging her consent was vitiated by her husband's misrepresentation of his age (actual DOB 1974 vs. represented 1981), a fact discovered post-marriage during registration. Her petition under Section 12(1)(c) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, was dismissed by the Family Court.

During the High Court appeal, both parties expressed unequivocal unwillingness to continue the marriage, formally seeking mutual dissolution. The wife additionally sought permanent alimony and return of gold ornaments, contingent on withdrawing other pending criminal and domestic violence cases. However, these ancillary claims introduced complex factual disputes not adjudicated at the trial level.

The High Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the Family Court's order. Instead of granting nullity as originally prayed, it issued a decree of divorce, reflecting a pragmatic judicial approach to the parties' mutual disinterest. Crucially, the court rejected the wife's claim for permanent alimony, reaffirming that Section 25 of the HMA mandates a separate application, a procedural requirement not met. Disputes regarding ornaments and settlement, being unpleaded and unproven below, could not be adjudicated in appeal. The wife was granted liberty to pursue these remedies in appropriate forums, including her DVC. This judgment underscores the necessity of procedural diligence for ancillary reliefs and the judiciary's evolving focus on the practical reality of marital breakdown.

title: Regulating Environmental Compliance Through Product-Specific Standards: A Critical Examination of the Proposed Ecomark Criteria for Paints, Batteries, Paper, and Allied Products
description:
India's Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change has proposed significant amendments (G.S.R. 452(E), 2026) to the Ecomark Rules, 2024, aiming to bolster environmental standards for manufactured products. This initiative, part of the broader LiFE Mission, updates the 1991 Ecomark scheme and entrusts the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) and Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) with its implementation. The draft notification is open for a 60-day public consultation to ensure participatory governance.

The proposed amendments introduce stringent, product-specific criteria across six categories:

1. Paints, Varnishes & Powder Coatings: Mandates BIS compliance, environmental clearances, and QR codes for transparency. It sets strict limits on Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs), toxic heavy metals (e.g., mercury, lead), formaldehyde, and bans persistent organic pollutants. Manufacturers must use 25% renewable energy, comply with Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR), possess ISO 14001:2015 certification, and use recyclable packaging. 2. Batteries: Requires CPCB EPR portal registration and display. Limits mercury and cadmium, prohibits chlorine-based plastics in primary casings/packaging, and sets graduated mandates for domestically recycled lead (50-70%). Units must meet effluent/emission standards, reduce energy consumption by 20% (preferably renewable), and ensure proper waste disposal. 3. Paper & Paper Products: Emphasizes sustainable raw material sourcing (e.g., 60% non-wood, 80% wastepaper), elemental/total chlorine-free bleaching, and strict limits on absorbable organic halides. It prohibits carcinogenic biocides, bans PFAS/optical brightening agents in food-contact paper, mandates chemical recovery plants for zero black-liquor discharge, and requires online effluent/emission monitoring. Specific norms for freshwater and electricity consumption are also prescribed. 4. Wood & Wood Substitute Products: Demands 100% sustainably sourced wood (agro-forestry/certified), utilization of agricultural residues for biomass, and industrial by-products for gypsum boards. It promotes natural adhesives, limits non-biodegradable materials (banning plastic in furniture), restricts formaldehyde, heavy metals, and VOCs, and requires 100% waste material utilization. 5. Fire Extinguishers: Prohibits ozone-depleting substances, mandates Ecomark-certified paint, bans halogenated plastics, and requires over 90% recycled metal components. Products must list ingredients, comply with EPR, and use extinguishing agents free from heavy metals and fluorinated organic compounds. ISO 14001:2015 certification is also required. 6. Coir & Coir Products: Stipulates mechanical fibre extraction, traceable natural rubber, and strict limits on residual pesticides, heavy metals, and harmful dyes. It mandates 25-30% renewable energy use, rainwater harvesting, comprehensive effluent treatment for wet processing, 100% treated wastewater utilization, and cleaner fuels in operations. Packaging must be compostable/biodegradable with end-of-life recycling instructions.

These amendments collectively promote key themes: mandatory BIS and environmental clearances, digital transparency via QR codes, robust EPR compliance, ISO 14001 certification, renewable energy integration, stringent hazardous substance elimination, sustainable packaging, and circular economy principles. This comprehensive regulatory push is poised to significantly shape India's manufacturing environmental footprint, aligning it with national sustainability goals.

title: SARFAESI Action Under Judicial Scrutiny: DRT Chandigarh Awards Compensation to Auction Purchasers While Setting Aside Illegal Sale
description:
The Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT), Chandigarh, in *S.G.K. Industrial Corporation and Ors. v. Authorized Officer, Indian Bank and Ors.*, set aside an e-auction conducted by Indian Bank under the SARFAESI Act, emphasizing that the Act’s objective of expedited debt recovery does not supersede the mandatory procedural safeguards. The ruling highlights that expediency cannot justify arbitrary actions or overlook meticulous legislative requirements.

The Bank's enforcement actions were marred by significant procedural irregularities. Crucially, it violated the mandatory 15-day notice period by publishing the sale notice on March 17th for an auction scheduled on March 29th. Furthermore, the Bank sold two distinct mortgaged plots belonging to different owners as a single unit, disadvantaging the borrowers by potentially reducing buyer interest and value. Other lapses included ignoring a higher One Time Settlement (OTS) proposal of Rs. 42 lacs from the borrowers, choosing instead to sell the property for Rs. 33.52 lacs, and failing to properly serve notices to the legal heirs of a deceased guarantor.

The Tribunal found the Bank's conduct "clumsy" and the auction fundamentally flawed. It underscored that previous failed auction attempts do not excuse non-compliance with statutory provisions, particularly the 15-day notice period, citing precedents from the Supreme Court and the Punjab and Haryana High Court. While acknowledging the auction purchasers as bona fide, the DRT clarified that the principle protecting confirmed auctions (the Bafna principle) does not extend to sales vitiated by cumulative and fundamental procedural irregularities.

Consequently, the DRT set aside the illegal auction. It directed Indian Bank to refund the entire sale consideration, stamp duty, and registration charges to the auction purchasers, along with 12% interest per annum. Additionally, recognizing the inconvenience caused by the Bank's illegal acts, the Tribunal awarded Rs. 30 lacs in compensation to the auction purchasers. The Bank was granted liberty to conduct a fresh auction in strict compliance with all statutory requirements, reaffirming robust judicial oversight in SARFAESI proceedings.

title: Delegation Without Abdication : The Regulatory Architecture of SEBI’s Outsourcing Guidelines
description:
SEBI's Circular CIR/MIRSD/24/2011 comprehensively governs outsourcing by registered intermediaries, issued due to increasing reliance on third parties without adequate risk frameworks. Defining outsourcing broadly to include intra-group arrangements, the guidelines address critical risks such as loss of control, data security, business continuity, and investor protection, drawing from IOSCO principles.

The circular strictly prohibits outsourcing of core business and compliance functions, like fund management or KYC. It establishes eight binding principles. Key among these are the mandatory formulation of a comprehensive outsourcing policy by the intermediary's Board, and the establishment of a robust risk management program assessing materiality and third-party capabilities. Crucially, the guidelines assert that outsourcing does not diminish the intermediary's obligations or accountability to clients and regulators; full liability for outsourced activities remains with the intermediary, and SEBI retains unimpeded access to third-party operations.

Further principles mandate thorough due diligence on third parties, formalization of arrangements through legally binding contracts, and the implementation of business continuity and contingency plans. Intermediaries must also ensure the protection of confidential information and mitigate systemic concentration risk when a single third party serves multiple entities. Additionally, intermediaries remain responsible for reporting suspicious transactions and were directed to self-assess existing arrangements.

Legally, the framework embodies a doctrine of non-delegable accountability, meaning intermediaries cannot use third-party failures as a defense. This rigor extends to related-party outsourcing, preventing circumvention of governance requirements and extending SEBI’s supervisory perimeter. In conclusion, SEBI's guidelines ensure that operational efficiencies gained from outsourcing do not compromise market integrity or investor protection, reinforcing that delegation of functions is not an abdication of regulatory responsibility.

title: Equity Prevails: When Conduct Speaks Louder Than the Register of Members
description:
The Supreme Court, in Dr. Bais Surgical and Medical Institute Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. v. Dhananjay Pande, delivered a significant ruling affirming that the absence of a formal entry in the register of members does not automatically preclude a person from maintaining a petition for relief from oppression and mismanagement under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956. This judgment emphasizes the primacy of equitable considerations and cumulative factual conduct over mere procedural formalities in determining locus standi.

The case involved Dhananjay Pande, who invested capital into Dr. Bais Surgical and Medical Institute. He was subsequently appointed Managing Director, and the hospital was rebranded using his trading concern's name, signifying recognition of his proprietary interest. Pande claimed shares were allotted but not formally entered in the company's register. Disputes arose, leading to his filing of company petitions alleging oppression and mismanagement.

The appellants contended that membership was exclusively defined by Section 41, requiring a formal agreement and entry in the register, and that this constituted a jurisdictional fact. Pande countered that the company's consistent conduct, accepting and utilizing his investment, appointing him MD, and renaming the hospital, unequivocally demonstrated his recognized proprietary interest, and the company should not benefit from its own default in registering his shares.

The Court critically examined Sections 2(27) and 41, concluding that the broader definition of "member" in Section 2(27) governs the locus standi for Sections 397 and 398, rather than being confined solely to the procedural requirements of Section 41. It reaffirmed the equitable character of these provisions. The Court found that Pande had been consistently recognized as a co-owner through contemporaneous correspondence, conciliation proceedings, his induction as Managing Director, and the rebranding of the hospital.

This landmark decision establishes that where a company's sustained conduct demonstrates long-standing recognition of a person's proprietary stake through correspondence, dealings, and financial arrangements, equity and justice mandate treating such person as a "member" for oppression and mismanagement proceedings, irrespective of a formal register entry. It significantly reinforces protections for minority investors and prevents companies from exploiting procedural defaults to defeat substantive shareholder rights.

title: Alpha Corp Development Private Limited v. Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority & Others
description:
The Supreme Court, in a significant ruling on May 5, 2026, restored project-specific resolution plans previously set aside by the NCLAT in the insolvency case of Earth Infrastructures Limited (EIL). The Court emphasized project-specific Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) for real estate, applied the doctrine of lifting the corporate veil, and curtailed penal claims by the Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority (GNIDA) due to its persistent inaction.

EIL, the corporate debtor, developed multiple projects through subsidiary companies on land leased by GNIDA. EIL held dominant stakes and managed these projects, while subsidiaries were mere conduits. The NCLT had approved resolution plans for these projects, but NCLAT overturned them, arguing the lands belonged to subsidiaries and required GNIDA's consent for transfer, also criticizing GNIDA's delayed claims.

The Supreme Court found it an apt case for lifting the corporate veil, recognizing the subsidiaries as extensions of EIL given their lack of independent business and EIL's control. It deemed GNIDA disentitled from levying penal interest and charges, citing the public trust doctrine and its institutional negligence in monitoring projects and failing to participate in CIRP. The Court also reaffirmed that under IBC Section 25A(3A), a class vote by an authorized representative binds all minority homebuyers, preventing individual challenges.

The Court allowed appeals by resolution applicants Alpha and Roma, restoring their plans. GNIDA was directed to recalculate dues based solely on principal amounts, excluding penal charges, to be paid over 24 months without additional interest. This judgment reinforces project-specific CIRP, the application of corporate veil in IBC, accountability for public authorities' inaction, and the finality of class-based voting in insolvency proceedings.

title: Down Syndrome and the National Trust Act: Kerala High Court Clarifies the Law on Legal Guardianship
description:
The Kerala High Court, in a significant judgment on June 3, 2026 (W.P.(C) No. 12482 of 2025), ruled that Down Syndrome constitutes "mental retardation" under the National Trust for the Welfare of Persons with Autism, Cerebral Palsy, Mental Retardation and Multiple Disabilities Act, 1999. This decision affirms a parent's right to seek legal guardianship for an adult child with Down Syndrome under the Act's protective framework, overturning an arbitrary administrative rejection.

The case stemmed from a father's application to be appointed as the legal guardian of his adult daughter, who was certified with Down Syndrome and 55% intellectual disability. The District Collector had summarily rejected the application, asserting that Down Syndrome was not a recognized disability under the Act. The petitioner argued that Down Syndrome, being a well-established cause of intellectual impairment, clearly falls within the definition of "mental retardation" as per Section 2(g) of the Act, and that the rejection was procedurally unsound due to lack of a hearing.

The Court's analysis meticulously examined statutory provisions and relied on authoritative medical literature, including the IAP Handbook and research reports from AIIMS, to establish that Down Syndrome inherently manifests as intellectual disability and sub-normality of intelligence, aligning with the Act's definition of "mental retardation." Furthermore, the Court found the District Collector's rejection to be procedurally flawed, having failed to comply with mandatory statutory requirements for scrutinizing applications, collecting materials, assessing the individual, and hearing all interested parties before making a decision.

Consequently, the High Court quashed the District Collector's rejection order and directed the reconsideration of the guardianship application within three months. This landmark judgment clarifies a crucial interpretive gap, providing much-needed legal recognition and support for families of persons with Down Syndrome, while simultaneously reinforcing the non-negotiable principle of procedural fairness in administrative proceedings concerning vulnerable individuals.

title: Rewriting the Rules of Resolution: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Act, 2026 and What It Changes
description:
India's Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016, has received its most comprehensive overhaul with the 2026 Amendment Act. This landmark legislation addresses a decade of identified structural gaps, growing cross-border insolvency complexities, and the urgent need to resolve stalled real estate projects. Receiving Presidential assent on April 6, 2026, and largely commenced on May 26, 2026, the Act significantly reshapes India's insolvency framework.

Key amendments include the introduction of a new Creditor-Initiated Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP). This mechanism enables notified financial institutions to initiate resolution for eligible corporate debtors without immediate Adjudicating Authority intervention, preserving a debtor-in-possession model for less complex entities. Critically, the Act empowers the Central Government to establish a statutory Group Insolvency framework for interconnected corporate entities and formulate cross-border insolvency rules, aligning India with international best practices.

Further reforms streamline liquidation processes through enhanced creditor supervision and clearer asset disposal guidelines. Procedural timelines for resolution and adjudication are tightened, and the Act clarifies avoidance transactions and fraudulent trading, expanding look-back periods. The regulatory and penalty architecture is reformed, largely shifting from criminal to civil penalties, and the "clean-slate" principle is strengthened by protecting licenses post-plan approval and extinguishing pre-approval claims, fostering investor confidence.

While the legislative architecture for new mechanisms like the Creditor-Initiated CIRP and Group Insolvency is now in place, their full operationalization awaits separate government notifications and subordinate legislation. This staged commencement reflects a deliberate strategy to build necessary regulatory and judicial infrastructure. The 2026 Amendment Act unequivocally signals India's commitment to an efficient, equitable, and globally aligned insolvency regime.

title: Determination of Financial versus Operational Debt in Invoice Financing Transactions Under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
description:
The NCLT Amaravati, in Kushal Finnovation Capital Pvt. Ltd. v. Rajesh Chillale, addressed critical questions regarding the classification of invoice financing as financial or operational debt and the validity of unregistered security interests during the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP). Kushal Finnovation Capital Private Limited provided "Invoice Financing–Dual Borrower" facilities to cotton suppliers, with Kallam Brothers Cottons Private Limited (Corporate Debtor) acting as guarantor.

Kushal Finnovation initially filed a claim for Rs. 5.33 Crore, admitted as an unsecured financial creditor. It subsequently sought reclassification as a secured financial creditor, relying on a general lien clause (Clause 5.1) in the credit agreements. However, the Interim Resolution Professional (IRP) rejected this request, asserting the debt was operational (stemming from bill discounting for goods purchased by the CD) and that no valid, registered security interest existed, especially considering prior registered charges held by other banks.

The Tribunal framed two pivotal issues. On debt classification, it determined that since Kushal Finnovation's recovery was confined to specific financed assets (cotton and related receivables), the facility was effectively "non-recourse." Consequently, it did not fall under Section 5(8)(e) of the IBC as financial debt. Instead, viewing its true commercial substance as the discounting of trade invoices, the Tribunal classified it as operational debt under Section 5(21). Regarding security interest, the Tribunal found Clause 5.1, a general lien over unspecified assets, insufficient to create an identifiable, enforceable charge without proper registration, which serves as crucial public notice.

Ultimately, the NCLT dismissed the application, deferring the reclassification decision to the IRP. This judgment reinforces that commercial substance takes precedence over contractual nomenclature. It clarifies that non-recourse invoice financing constitutes operational debt and that secured creditor status cannot be claimed through unregistered, unperfected, or broadly worded contractual liens. Financiers in the trade finance ecosystem must ensure security interests are properly documented and registered to secure their claims during corporate insolvency.

title: CoC Autonomy Over CIRP Costs: NCLT Bengaluru on Interim Finance and Member Contribution
description:
The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) Bengaluru, in Gonugunta Murali v. Income Tax Department (15 April 2026), affirmed the Committee of Creditors' (CoC) paramount commercial wisdom regarding Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) funding, limiting judicial intervention. The Resolution Professional (RP) for Sai Krishna Minerals Pvt. Ltd. faced severe funding shortfalls for CIRP expenses. In its third meeting, the CoC, by a 67.25% majority, rejected direct member contributions and instead resolved to raise interim finance from external sources like banks or financial institutions.

Despite this CoC resolution, the approved interim finance did not materialize, forcing the RP to use personal funds. Consequently, the RP filed an application seeking NCLT direction to compel CoC members, including the Income Tax Department, to contribute proportionally. The Income Tax Department resisted, asserting it lacked statutory authority or budgetary provisions to fund private insolvency proceedings, and highlighted that the CoC had already approved an external financing model.

The NCLT, citing the Supreme Court's K. Sashidhar judgment, reiterated that the CoC's commercial wisdom is paramount and not amenable to judicial review. It held that the CoC's resolution to raise interim finance was valid and binding, exceeding the 66% approval threshold. The Tribunal also noted that compelling a Central Government Department to contribute lacked statutory basis and that the RP had not exhausted the CoC-approved alternative of seeking external finance. Therefore, the NCLT dismissed the RP's application, directing the RP to pursue the generation of interim finance from operational creditors, banks, or financial institutions as initially approved by the CoC. This ruling reinforces that judicial forums will not override the CoC's autonomous commercial decisions on CIRP funding, particularly when statutory creditors are involved and approved funding mechanisms remain unexplored.

title: Unilateral Institutional Invocation: A Façade That Cannot Cure the Vice of Interested Party Appointment in Arbitration
description:
The Calcutta High Court, in *L&T Finance Ltd. v. Jai Paras Material Store and Ors.*, affirmed that an interested party's unilateral invocation of an institutional mechanism cannot bypass statutory prohibitions against unilateral arbitrator appointments. Executing courts under Section 36 are empowered to refuse enforcement of awards stemming from such fundamental jurisdictional defects.

In this case, L&T Finance unilaterally referred a default dispute to Presolv360, an Online Dispute Resolution forum, for arbitrator appointment after the borrower's non-participation. An ex parte award was rendered, which L&T sought to enforce. The Court questioned the validity of an arbitration clause granting appointment power to an interested party, the legality of unilateral institutional invocation without consent, and the executing court's ability to address these fundamental issues.

The Court's analysis relied on Sections 12(5) and 14(1)(a) of the Arbitration Act, rendering interested parties ineligible and their mandates terminated. Citing Supreme Court precedents (*TRF Ltd., Perkins Eastman*), it underscored that an interested party cannot appoint an arbitrator, directly or indirectly, to ensure equal treatment (Section 18). Unilateral institutional invocation without mutual consent was deemed impermissible; Section 11 offers the exclusive remedy for neutral court appointment in non-participatory scenarios.

Crucially, the Court held that an award by a unilaterally appointed arbitrator is void ab initio, "non-est," lacking inherent jurisdiction. Such a fundamental defect, it affirmed, *must* be examined by an executing court under Section 36, irrespective of a Section 34 challenge, as no limitation cures a jurisdictional nullity. The execution petition was dismissed, the ex parte award declared unenforceable, with liberty for fresh, valid proceedings.

This judgment significantly reaffirms arbitral process integrity. It clarifies that executing courts must decline enforcement of awards suffering from such jurisdictional nullities, guiding financial institutions to utilize Section 11 court applications for non-participating respondents, rather than unilateral institutional invocation.

title: Section 29A Inapplicable Where Arbitration Invoked Prior To 2015 Amendment: Delhi High Court In Partnership Property Dispute
description:
The Delhi High Court, in Prem Lata Surekha v. Chakradhari Surekha, affirmed an arbitral award in a significant family partnership dispute, underscoring the limited scope of judicial interference in arbitration matters. The dispute originated from M/s Sri Narayan Rajkumar, a firm constituted in 1973 with a 1974 partnership deed containing an arbitration clause.

Following a partner's death in 2003, Chakradhari Surekha alleged exclusion from the firm and claimed Prem Lata Surekha had fabricated subsequent partnership deeds to unlawfully transfer a valuable industrial property. Prem Lata countered that Chakradhari had retired decades ago, and the original 1974 deed was no longer valid.

In 2015, Chakradhari invoked arbitration. The arbitral tribunal meticulously examined evidence and found Prem Lata's alleged subsequent deeds unproven, relying only on photocopies and conflicting official records. Concluding that Chakradhari's retirement was not established, the tribunal upheld the 1974 deed as valid and directed an equal division of the property between the two surviving partners.

The Single Judge of the Delhi High Court upheld this award. On appeal, the Division Bench rejected arguments that Section 29A of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act (introduced by the 2015 amendment, prescribing timelines for awards) applied retrospectively, as the arbitration was invoked before its enactment. The Court also noted that other stakeholders had either settled their claims or voluntarily withdrawn. Reiterating the principle that Sections 34 and 37 do not permit re-appreciation of evidence, the Division Bench dismissed the appeal and imposed costs due to the appellant's non-bona fide conduct. This judgment reinforces the sanctity of arbitral findings, the necessity of strict proof for partnership changes, and clarifies the non-retrospective application of Section 29A.

title: Section 29A Extension Maintainable Even After Mandate Termination, Parties Not to Blame for Arbitrator’s Failure to Pronounce Award: Himachal Pradesh High Court
description:
The Himachal Pradesh High Court, in Ramesh Chand v. National Highways Authority of India, has affirmed that applications filed under Section 29A(5) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, seeking an extension of time to conclude arbitration proceedings, are maintainable even after the arbitral tribunal's mandate has terminated by operation of law. The Court subsequently extended the time for the Arbitrator to conclude the proceedings until July 20, 2026.

The case originated from a land acquisition where the applicants, dissatisfied with an award, approached an Arbitrator. Arguments were heard and reserved, but the Arbitrator was transferred without pronouncing the award. The successor Arbitrator subsequently closed the proceedings, noting that the mandate had terminated under Section 29A(4) of the Act, granting liberty to parties to seek court intervention. The applicants then filed the present applications before the High Court.

The Court, relying on the Supreme Court's decision in Rohan Builders (India) Private Limited v. Berger Paints India Limited, reiterated that applications for extension under Section 29A(4) read with 29A(5) are maintainable even after the expiry of the statutory period. Finding that neither party was at fault for the Arbitrator's failure to pronounce the award post-reservation, and attributing the delay to administrative reasons, the Court determined there was sufficient cause for granting the extension. This ensures parties are not penalized for circumstances beyond their control.

title: Writ or Tribunal? The SARFAESI Crossroads for Auction Purchasers
description:
The Punjab and Haryana High Court, in Devi Hospitality Pvt. Ltd. v. Punjab National Bank & Anr., has definitively ruled that the Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT) under Section 17(1) of the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002 (SARFAESI Act), is the exclusive and efficacious forum for aggrieved auction purchasers, to the exclusion of writ jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution of India.

The petitioner, Devi Hospitality, emerged as the highest bidder in a PNB e-auction but encountered issues with the "Sale Confirmation Letter," citing deficiencies and subsequent allegations of fraudulent documentation by the bank. Despite depositing 25% of the bid amount, the petitioner sought an extension for the balance payment due to the COVID-19 pandemic. PNB, however, cancelled the sale and forfeited the Rs. 1.07 crore deposit, leading the petitioner to file a writ petition.

PNB contended that the writ petition was not maintainable, citing Supreme Court precedents like Agarwal Tracom Pvt. Ltd. v. Punjab National Bank. This case established that the forfeiture of an auction purchaser's deposit under SARFAESI Rules is an integral measure under Section 13(4) of the Act, challengeable solely before the DRT. The High Court, observing factual similarities to Agarwal Tracom, declined to adjudicate disputed facts in writ jurisdiction. It disposed of the petition, directing Devi Hospitality to approach the jurisdictional DRT within 45 days. The DRT was instructed to consider the application on its merits without dismissing it on grounds of limitation.

This judgment reinforces that the DRT is the designated and exclusive forum for challenging actions taken under the SARFAESI Act, including the forfeiture of deposits. It cautions against invoking extraordinary writ jurisdiction without first exhausting the available statutory remedies, which can lead to procedural delays and complications.

title: The Last Word Belongs to the Deceased: Kerala High Court on Body Donation Rights
description:
The Kerala High Court, in Greeny Tomy & Ors. v. State of Kerala & Ors., decisively affirmed the primacy of an individual's right to determine the disposition of their body after death, even over the objections of surviving family members. The case addressed a fundamental question of posthumous autonomy, ruling that a deceased person's clear wish to donate their body for medical education must be respected. This judgment underscores the extension of dignity and bodily integrity beyond life.

The dispute arose when some children of a deceased woman, Mary, sought to reclaim her body for traditional burial, alleging they were not informed of her decision to donate it. However, other family members presented a written consent executed by Mary under Section 4A of the Kerala Anatomy Act, 1957, unequivocally expressing her desire for body donation. The legal issue before the Court was whether family members' preferences could override such a documented declaration.

The Division Bench emphasized that while legal personality ordinarily ceases upon death, the law protects certain interests of the deceased, including their body. It held that a person's decision regarding their body's treatment after death is an integral aspect of their autonomy and dignity. Since the authenticity and voluntary nature of Mary's consent were undisputed, the Court found no legal basis to disregard her wishes. Familial preferences, while emotionally significant, could not supersede a valid and clearly expressed decision made by the deceased during her lifetime.

Ultimately, the Kerala High Court upheld the initial ruling, dismissing the appeal. The decision reinforces that an individual's informed choice regarding body donation is lawful and must be honoured, strengthening public confidence in donation programs and balancing private sentiments with the public interest in medical advancement. It sets a significant precedent for upholding self-determination beyond death.

title: Statutory Compliance Over Contractual Deviation: Telangana RERA Appellate Tribunal Upholds Penalty for Promoter’s Agreement Violation
description:
The Telangana RERA Appellate Tribunal, in Mehta & Modi Realty Kowkur LLP v. Deepa Suraj Premi, reinforced RERA's homebuyer protection mandate, upholding a penalty against a promoter for statutory violations and clarifying critical builder-buyer issues.

The dispute involved a promoter executing a sale agreement significantly deviating from the RERA-uploaded model (violating Rule 38). Homebuyers faced retrospective maintenance charges pre-possession via a prematurely formed, fraudulent "Greenwood Welfare Association." Other issues included demands for interest on delayed payments (during construction halts, on GST/TDS), and separate water charges, despite the project lacking an occupancy certificate.

The Regulatory Authority imposed a Rs. 10,99,992/- penalty for false information (Section 60 RERA). It directed maintenance payable only post-possession, dissolution of the existing association for a new one under the Telangana Cooperative Societies Act, and clarified GST applies solely to sale consideration, not interest.

The Appellate Tribunal affirmed this decision. It ruled that the agreement deviation violated Rule 38, justifying the penalty. Maintenance charges are statutory liabilities only post-possession, overriding non-compliant contractual terms. The Tribunal mandated association formation under the Telangana Cooperative Societies Act post-occupancy certificate and 60% allottee possession, upholding the existing entity's dissolution. While allowing water charges (utility security deposits), it disallowed interest on delayed payments due to incompleteness and clarified GST's scope.

This judgment underscores the supremacy of statutory compliance, dismissing the promoter's appeal and upholding homebuyer protection against RERA mandate circumvention.

title: Eureka Forbes Ltd. v. Indian Railway Catering and Tourism Corporation: Reaffirming Fairness in Arbitral Proceedings
description:
The Delhi High Court, in Eureka Forbes Ltd. v. Indian Railway Catering and Tourism Corporation, reaffirmed that arbitral tribunals' procedural discretion must align with natural justice and fairness. The judgment critically examined the treatment of counterclaims when a party is proceeded against ex parte and clarified the distinction between a procedural order and an interim arbitral award.

The dispute arose from a Licence Agreement, leading to arbitration where Eureka Forbes filed a counterclaim. Following Eureka Forbes' non-appearance at two consecutive hearings, the Arbitrator proceeded ex parte against the company and rejected its counterclaim. He subsequently refused to restore the counterclaim, deeming its rejection a final determination beyond his jurisdiction.

Eureka Forbes challenged these orders under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The High Court determined that the ex parte order was merely procedural and thus not challengeable as an interim award. However, applying a threefold test (final adjudication of a substantive claim, binding consequences, and the tribunal becoming functus officio regarding that issue), the Court concluded that the rejection of the counterclaim was an interim award. This rejection effectively brought a substantive claim to an end without adjudication on merits, violating statutory principles of fairness and equal treatment (Sections 18 and 25 of the Act).

The Court emphasized that mere non-appearance does not automatically justify dismissing an already filed counterclaim. Such claims should be adjudicated on available material, as procedural defaults should not lead to the forfeiture of substantive rights. Setting aside the interim award, the Delhi High Court restored the counterclaim for adjudication, thereby reinforcing that arbitration must uphold fairness, equality, and due process, ensuring meaningful access to justice.

title: Judicial Restraint under Section 34: Delhi High Court Upholds Arbitral Tribunal’s Refusal of Specific Performance
description:
The Delhi High Court, in Imran Ahmed Ansari & Anr. v. Intex Technologies (India) Ltd. & Anr., reaffirmed the narrow scope of judicial interference with arbitral awards under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The judgment guides on specific performance, patent illegality, and the limits of court intervention in arbitration. The dispute arose from an Agreement to Sell an industrial plot where the Arbitral Tribunal declined specific performance, instead directing sellers to refund ₹3.50 crores with 15% interest and reimburse transfer charges.

Aggrieved by the denial of specific performance, the purchasers challenged the award, arguing the Tribunal incorrectly applied Section 10 of the Specific Relief Act, which presumes specific performance for immovable property. They contended their readiness to perform was ignored.

The High Court reiterated that Section 34 is not an appellate forum and prohibits re-appreciation of evidence or substitution of the court's view for the arbitrator's. It emphasized that an award can only be set aside for fundamental legal defects, such as patent illegality, not merely a different interpretation of facts or law. The Court found the Tribunal had consciously considered Section 10 and reasonably concluded that monetary compensation was adequate, given the transaction's commercial nature.

Upholding the award, the Court found the Tribunal's decision plausible and legally sustainable. It also affirmed the Tribunal's reasoning regarding the sellers' misrepresentation, the adequacy of reasons in the award, and the rejection of an alleged cash payment as being outside the arbitration scope. Dismissing the petition, the Delhi High Court underscored India's pro-arbitration stance, reinforcing minimal judicial intervention and the autonomy of the arbitral process, positioning Section 34 as a supervisory remedy rather than an appellate one.

title: Dark Patterns in Ed-Tech: CCPA Imposes Penalty on PhysicsWallah
description:
India's Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has levied a Rs. 5,00,000 penalty on ed-tech giant PhysicsWallah (PW) for deploying manipulative "dark patterns" on its platform. This landmark decision (Case No. CCPA-2/94/2025-CCPA, Order dated 1 June 2026) marks a significant enforcement of the 2023 Dark Patterns Guidelines, specifically addressing their application in the vulnerable ed-tech sector, which serves numerous minor students.

The CCPA identified three core violations. First, PW engaged in "Basket Sneaking" by automatically adding a pre-selected Rs. 10 donation to the 'PW Foundation' during checkout. Over 21 lakh users were affected, leading to approximately Rs. 2.47 crore collected. Second, "Confirm Shaming" was used, where descriptions of the foundation’s charitable work alongside the pre-selected donation emotionally pressured users to retain the charge. Third, PW committed "Forced Action" by mandatorily requiring mobile numbers and email addresses for "free" courses, despite no evidence of personalized service, thus subverting consumer choice.

Despite initial denials, PW later admitted the donation feature operated from February 2024 to December 2025. The CCPA emphasized that such practices violate the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, and E-Commerce Rules, particularly concerning vulnerable consumer groups like students. The order directs PW to cease these dark patterns, refund the collected donation amounts, and pay the penalty.

This ruling underscores that charitable elements in transactions must be genuine opt-ins, and "free" offers must disclose all access conditions upfront. It sets a crucial compliance benchmark for digital platforms, stressing that even individually small, systemically deployed manipulative practices affecting a large consumer base carry substantial regulatory risk, prioritizing consumer autonomy and informed consent over mere transparency.

title: Procedural Non-Compliance and Limitation Defeat Bank’s SARFAESI Action: An Analysis of the Gopu Bala Reddy v. Union Bank of India Ruling
description:
The Debt Recovery Tribunal, Hyderabad, in `Gopu Bala Reddy v. Union Bank of India`, underscored the mandatory nature of procedural compliance and limitation periods under the SARFAESI Act. The ruling invalidated Union Bank of India's enforcement actions against guarantors for a loan, citing multiple legal breaches.

Crucially, the Tribunal found the bank failed to serve the principal borrower (M/s BRG Energy Limited, undergoing liquidation) with the mandatory Section 13(2) demand notice. This rendered subsequent measures void ab initio, emphasizing that borrower notification is essential even when pursuing guarantors.

Further procedural infirmities included non-compliance with Rule 8 of the Security Interest Rules for possession and sale notices. The bank published in an obscure newspaper, failed to provide proof of affixture for notices, and lacked valuation reports for the property, raising concerns of potential collusion due to the sole bidder.

Significantly, the Tribunal upheld the limitation defense. The loan was classified as NPA on December 31, 2011. The 12-year period under Article 62 of the Limitation Act for mortgage enforcement expired on December 31, 2023. Thus, the bank's fresh demand notice in March 2024 was time-barred under Section 36 of SARFAESI, rejecting COVID-19 exclusion arguments.

The DRT allowed the application, declaring the bank's measures void, setting aside the sale, and ordering a refund. This judgment is pivotal, reinforcing that SARFAESI powers are not unbridled and demand strict adherence to statutory procedures and limitation, profoundly influencing future enforcement strategies for secured creditors.

title: Arbitration Cannot Be Founded on Unilateral Acknowledgement: Delhi High Court Reaffirms Consent as the Basis of Arbitral Jurisdiction
description:
The Delhi High Court, in Matsya Fincap Pvt. Ltd. v. Govind Lal, ruled that a valid arbitration agreement, foundational to arbitral jurisdiction under Section 7 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, cannot be based solely on a unilateral acknowledgement letter. Such a document, signed by only one party and lacking contemporaneous evidence of mutual assent, is insufficient. Consequently, an ex-parte award based on it was deemed a nullity, incapable of enforcement. This judgment is crucial for finance companies and commercial entities, underscoring that consent forms the very source of an arbitrator's authority.

In the case, Matsya Fincap sought to execute an ex-parte award against Govind Lal, which was founded on a receipt-cum-acknowledgement letter. This letter, containing an arbitration clause and naming a specific arbitrator, was admittedly signed only by Govind Lal. The High Court emphasized that Section 7 mandates both a written agreement and consensus ad idem (mutual assent). It found the letter failed Section 7(4)(a) as it wasn't signed by both parties, and Section 7(4)(b) as no mutual communications evidencing agreement were produced. The mere presence of an arbitration clause in a unilaterally signed document is inadequate to establish a valid arbitration agreement.

The Court further held that the acknowledgement letter did not constitute a concluded, enforceable contract, lacking bilateral assent and essential contractual elements. A crucial aspect was the arbitrator's erroneous factual premise that the document bore both parties' signatures, which critically invalidated the arbitral jurisdiction. The High Court clarified that an executing court can refuse to enforce an award that is void ab initio due to inherent lack of jurisdiction, rejecting the appellant's argument for Section 34 challenge exclusivity.
